newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK budget seen denting Labour's lead.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK budget seen denting Labour's lead.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative party is still heading for a hefty defeat at the next general election, but last week's budget may have cushioned the blow to some degree, according to a Reuters poll published on Monday.

Election experts and political analysts polled in December's update of the Reuters monthly election survey predicted on average that the opposition Labour party would win with an overall majority of 36 seats -- three seats fewer than their November predictions.
Although fiscally prudent, the budget may have persuaded some floating voters to switch to the beleaguered Conservatives.

"The budget was electorally quite skilful because it didn't look like a cynical bribe, but it would have enforced the impression that the Conservatives are the tax-cutting party," said Ivor Crewe, vice-chancellor at the University of Essex.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (Finance Minister) Kenneth Clarke, in his last budget before an election, was eager to restore the image of the Conservatives as the party most able to manage the economy competently.
"It (the budget) marginally increases the Tories' chances. Clarke is promoting the image of responsible management of the economy," said John Benyon at the University of Leicester.

Benyon added that clever timing of budget measures could also help Conservative election chances. "A lot of the negative signs won't be felt until after the election, whereas the penny off income tax will arrive just before," he said.
Most of the 20 experts still predicted a May 1997 election. The last possible day is May 22, but many pin-pointed May 1 because it coincides with local elections that day.

The survey showed Labour would probably occupy 345 seats of the 659 available at the next parliament while the Conservatives would get 262. Liberal Democrats would have 25 seats and 'others', which include the Scottish National Party (SNP) and Ulster Unionists, would take 27 seats.
Since the Conservatives had played most of their high cards in their annual annual conference and the Queen's speech, many analysts reckoned the budget was the last ace up the party's sleeve.

Disappointingly for the government, Tuesday's giveaways received a lukewarm response from both voters and financial markets, and any resultant gain in the polls would only allow them to play catch-up.
Clarke trimmed a penny of the basic rate of income tax to 23 pence but increased taxes on petrol, cigarettes and air travel.

"The Tories (Conservatives) need a political miracle and one of the opportunities for that was the budget, but I don't think it goes anywhere near fulfilling that requirement," said Michael Thrasher at the University of Plymouth.
Others experts said the budget could have damaged the Conservatives' re-election prospects further.
Recent opinion polls show Labour's lead at between 15 and 28.9 percent, but analysts predict the gap to narrow as the Conservative campaign machine leaps into action.
